claim: Infection with Influenza A virus (IAV) causes fever, loss of appetite, and excessive sleepiness.
source: Infection with Influenza A virus (IAV) causes the well-known symptoms of the flu, including fever, loss of appetite, and excessive sleepiness.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about IAV symptoms presented in the abstract.

claim: Symptoms of IAV infection are mediated by the brain.
source: These responses, mediated by the brain, will normally disappear once the virus is cleared from the system, but a severe respiratory virus infection may cause long-lasting neurological disturbances.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: A severe respiratory virus infection may cause long-lasting neurological disturbances including encephalitis lethargica and narcolepsy.
source: These responses, mediated by the brain, will normally disappear once the virus is cleared from the system, but a severe respiratory virus infection may cause long-lasting neurological disturbances. These include encephalitis lethargica and narcolepsy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The mechanisms behind long-lasting neurological changes after IAV infection are unknown.
source: The mechanisms behind such long lasting changes are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: The hypothalamus is a central regulator of the homeostatic response during a viral challenge.
source: The hypothalamus is a central regulator of the homeostatic response during a viral challenge.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Mice were intranasally infected with an H1N1 virus and the brain was extracted at different time points.
source: To gain insight into the neuronal and non-neuronal molecular changes during an IAV infection, we intranasally infected mice with an H1N1 virus and extracted the brain at different time points.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of the hypothalamus was used to identify transcriptional effects in all identified cell populations.
source: Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) of the hypothalamus, we identify transcriptional effects in all identified cell populations.
evidence: This describes the methodology and findings of the study.

claim: The most pronounced transcriptional response was at 3 days post infection, with a strong downregulation of genes across all cell types.
source: The snRNA-seq data showed the most pronounced transcriptional response at 3 days past infection, with a strong downregulation of genes across all cell types.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: General immune processes were mainly impacted in microglia during IAV infection.
source: General immune processes were mainly impacted in microglia, the brain resident immune cells, where we found increased numbers of cells expressing pro-inflammatory gene networks.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Increased numbers of microglia cells expressing pro-inflammatory gene networks were found during IAV infection.
source: General immune processes were mainly impacted in microglia, the brain resident immune cells, where we found increased numbers of cells expressing pro-inflammatory gene networks.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Most neuronal cell populations downregulated genes contributing to energy homeostasis in mitochondria and protein translation in the cytosol.
source: In addition, we found that most neuronal cell populations downregulated genes contributing to the energy homeostasis in mitochondria and protein translation in the cytosol, indicating potential reduced cellular and neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the snRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Downregulation of genes in neuronal cells might be a preventive mechanism to avoid intracellular viral replication and attack by phagocytosing cells.
source: This might be a preventive mechanism in neuronal cells to avoid intracellular viral replication and attack by phagocytosing cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the abstract.

claim: The change of microglia gene activity suggests a shift in microglia activity to provide increased surveillance of their surroundings.
source: The change of microglia gene activity suggest that this is complemented by a shift in microglia activity to provide increased surveillance of their surroundings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented in the abstract.

source: Beyond seasonal epidemics, H1N1 IAV strains have been identified as the causal agent for the pandemics in 1918 and 2009, leading up to 50 million and 18,000 deaths worldwide, respectively (Simonsen et al., 2013; Taubenberger and Morens, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The 1918 H1N1 pandemic led to up to 50 million deaths worldwide.

claim: The 2009 H1N1 pandemic led to 18,000 deaths worldwide.

source: A peak in new narcolepsy cases was also seen following the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, and while this was linked with the Pandemrix vaccine in Europe, in China it was unrelated to vaccinations and thus might instead be linked to infection with the virus itself (Ahmed et al., 2014; Han et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The peak in narcolepsy cases following the 2009 H1N1 pandemic was linked with the Pandemrix vaccine in Europe.

evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some IAV strains are considered neurotropic, meaning they hold the machinery to infiltrate the CNS and replicate.
source: Some IAV strains are considered neurotropic, meaning that they hold the machinery to infiltrate the CNS and replicate, but evidence suggest that even non-neurotropic influenza strains can infiltrate the brain and cause neurological disturbances (Ekstrand, 2012; Hodgson et al., 2012; Macias et al., 2021; Majde et al., 2007; Zielinski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Even non-neurotropic influenza strains can infiltrate the brain and cause neurological disturbances.
source: Some IAV strains are considered neurotropic, meaning that they hold the machinery to infiltrate the CNS and replicate, but evidence suggest that even non-neurotropic influenza strains can infiltrate the brain and cause neurological disturbances (Ekstrand, 2012; Hodgson et al., 2012; Macias et al., 2021; Majde et al., 2007; Zielinski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: When non-neurotropic viruses are found in the CNS, they are either not able to replicate at all or not efficiently in the brain resident cells.
source: When non-neurotropic viruses are found in the CNS, they are either not able to replicate at all or not efficiently in the brain resident cells (Hosseini et al., 2018; Zielinski et al., 2013).

claim: The H1N1 strain from the 2009 pandemic (H1N1 pdm09) is non-neurotropic.
source: The H1N1 strain from the 2009 pandemic (H1N1 pdm09) is non-neurotropic (Sadasivan et al., 2015), so the mechanism behind the neurological consequences seen after that H1N1 infection must be caused by indirect effects rather than direct viral infection of brain cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The mechanism behind the neurological consequences seen after H1N1 pdm09 infection must be caused by indirect effects rather than direct viral infection of brain cells.
source: The H1N1 strain from the 2009 pandemic (H1N1 pdm09) is non-neurotropic (Sadasivan et al., 2015), so the mechanism behind the neurological consequences seen after that H1N1 infection must be caused by indirect effects rather than direct viral infection of brain cells.

claim: Cytokines produced during a peripheral infection can reach the brain and cause functional disturbances.
source: It is well known that cytokines produced during a peripheral infection can reach the brain and cause functional disturbances (Dantzer and Kelley, 2007).

claim: Microglia become activated during peripheral IAV infections with non-neurotropic strains.
source: It has also been shown that microglia become activated during peripheral IAV infections with non-neurotropic strains. Whether this microglia activation is a neuroprotective mechanism or contributes to neuroinflammation and -degeneration remains elusive (Dusedau et al., 2021; Sadasivan et al., 2015; Wiley et al., 2015).

source: It has also been shown that microglia become activated during peripheral IAV infections with non-neurotropic strains. Whether this microglia activation is a neuroprotective mechanism or contributes to neuroinflammation and -degeneration remains elusive (Dusedau et al., 2021; Sadasivan et al., 2015; Wiley et al., 2015).

source: The hypothalamus is a functional integrator of peripheral signals and regulates several physiological and behavioural functions via several specialised nuclei (Berthoud and Münzberg, 2011; Bonnavion et al., 2016; Stuber and Wise, 2016).

claim: Different hypothalamic neuron populations control feeding, body temperature, sleep-wake states, and circadian rhythms.

claim: The lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) contains hypocretin (HCRT) or melanin-concentrating hormone releasing (MCH) neurons.

source: These neurons are coupled to several biological functions including metabolism and the regulation of sleep and wake states (Oesch and Adamantidis, 2021).
